{{Short description|British-Canadian academic (1939–2022)}}
{{Use British English|date=November 2017}}
{{Use dmy dates|date=June 2026}}
'''John K. S. McKay''' ({{IPAc-en|m|ə|ˈ|k|aɪ}} {{respell|mə|KYE}}; 18 November 1939 – 19 April 2022)<ref>[https://www.crmath.ca/en/2022/04/27/john-mckay-1939-2022/ John McKay (1939–2022), CRM News, Centre de recherches mathématiques, Université de Montréal]</ref><ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.crm.umontreal.ca/en/index.shtml |title=John McKay (1939–2022) |access-date=22 April 2022 |archive-date=14 February 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220214175236/http://www.crm.umontreal.ca/en/index.shtml |url-status=dead }}</ref><ref>{{Cite AV media |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5Mg25JK31wE |title=Monstrous moonshine |date=2020-06-07 |last=Richard E Borcherds |access-date=2026-05-21 |via=YouTube}}</ref> was a British-Canadian mathematician and academic who worked at [[Concordia University (Quebec)|Concordia University]], known for his discovery of [[monstrous moonshine]], his joint construction of some [[sporadic simple group]]s, for the [[McKay conjecture]] in representation theory, and for the [[McKay correspondence]] relating certain [[finite group]]s to [[Lie group]]s.

==Biography==
McKay was educated at [[Dulwich College]], earned his Bachelor and Diploma in 1961 and 1962 at the [[University of Manchester]], and his PhD in 1971 from the [[University of Edinburgh]].<ref>{{Cite book|date=1970|title=Computing with finite groups|hdl=1842/6615|last=McKay|first=John K. S.|type=Ph.D. thesis|publisher=University of Edinburgh}}</ref><ref name=phd>{{MathGenealogy|id=94551}}</ref>
Since 1974 he worked at [[Concordia University]], since 1979 as a professor in computer science.

He was elected a fellow of the [[Royal Society of Canada]] in 2000, and won the 2003 [[CRM-Fields-PIMS prize]].

In April 2007 a Joint Conference was organised by the [[Université de Montréal]] and Concordia University honouring four decades of McKay's work.
